NEWBORN 1 · LESSON 1

High-Contrast Cards for Newborns

Age Birth–6 WeeksSubject SeeClass Newborn 1Time 2–5 minutes

Newborns see the world in bold shapes long before they see details. These twelve black and white baby flashcards use strong, high-contrast patterns — circles, stripes, checkerboards and friendly faces — because bold contrast is exactly what catches a brand-new baby’s attention. It is the classic newborn visual stimulation activity, turned into a calm two-to-five-minute class: no printing, no setup, just you, your baby and one card at a time.

Show a card, watch, talk softly, and stop when your baby is done. That is the whole class. Nothing to teach and nothing to test — just an easy first step into Kiddo.school, from birth onward.

TEACHER’S LESSON

How this class is taught.

By the end of this class: your baby has focused on bold black-and-white shapes, followed one slow movement with their eyes, and told you — by looking longer or looking away — which pictures they love.

  1. 01
    Welcome

    “Hello, little one. It is looking time — ready?”

    How: Hold your baby facing you, and hold the first card 20–30 cm from their face — about the distance from your elbow to your fingers.

  2. Look and learn, one shape at a time
  3. 02
    Card 1 · Circle

    “Look — a circle! A big, round, black circle.”

    How: Say circle slowly, twice. Newborns learn by hearing the same calm word while the shape fills their eyes.

  4. 03
    Card 2 · Square

    “Now a square — one, two, three, four sides.”

    How: Trace the air along one edge with your finger. The slow movement pulls their gaze onto the shape.

  5. 04
    Card 3 · Stripes up

    “Stripes! Up and down, up and down.”

    How: Run your finger down one stripe. Bold lines are the easiest thing for brand-new eyes to follow.

  6. 05
    Card 4 · Stripes across

    “And sideways stripes — zoom, across we go.”

    How: Move your finger left to right once, slowly. That sideways track is the first rep of visual tracking.

  7. 06
    Card 5 · Checkerboard

    “A checkerboard — black, white, black, white.”

    How: Point to one black square, then one white square. Contrast is exactly what newborn eyes see best.

  8. 07
    Card 6 · Circles in circles

    “Circles inside circles — all the way in.”

    How: Trace one slow finger lap from the outside in, then stop and wait. Waiting is part of the teaching.

  9. 08
    Card 7 · Spiral

    “A spiral — round and round and in.”

    How: Let your finger follow the spiral once. If their eyes follow, that is tracking — cheer softly.

  10. 09
    Card 8 · Triangle

    “A triangle — point at the top!”

    How: Tap the point gently. Naming the sharpest part gives your baby one clear place to look.

  11. 10
    Card 9 · Target

    “A target — dot, ring, dot.”

    How: Name the middle, then the ring, then the middle again. One name at a time keeps it calm.

  12. 11
    Card 10 · Eyes

    “Hello, eyes! Can you see me?”

    How: Hold the card still and wait. When a newborn stares hard, they are studying — let them study.

  13. 12
    Card 11 · Face

    “A smiling face! Hello, face.”

    How: Say hello the way you would to a person. Faces are a newborn’s favourite picture in the world.

  14. 13
    Card 12 · Symmetrical face

    “And another face — hello again!”

    How: Finish by holding this card while you talk. Your real face next to the card doubles the lesson.

  15. 14
    Practice

    “Which one does my baby love best?”

    How: Show the two cards your baby looked at longest, one more time each. Repeating a favourite is the newborn version of practice.

  16. 15
    Check

    “All done — was that nice?”

    How: The check is reading your baby: wide eyes and stillness means more, yawning or looking away means finished. Both answers are correct.

  17. 16
    Well done

    “Great looking today. See you tomorrow, same time.”

    How: Two minutes of full attention is a complete newborn class. Stop while it is still fun, and tomorrow they come back hungry for more.

Read the script while you show the cards above — the say-lines are yours to say out loud and the how-lines quietly explain the trick behind each step. Skip, shorten or repeat anything: the class bends to your child, never the other way round.

PARENT INSTRUCTIONS

How to use these cards

  1. 01

    Hold the card close

    Hold the card about 8–12 inches (20–30 cm) from your baby’s face — roughly the distance from your elbow to your fingers. Close, bold and steady is easiest for brand-new eyes.

  2. 02

    Let your baby look

    Let your baby study the image. Some babies stare hard, some go very still, some wiggle with excitement. All of that counts as looking.

  3. 03

    Move it slowly

    When your baby is alert and interested, slowly move a card from side to side, a few centimetres each way, and watch their eyes follow.

  4. 04

    Stop in time

    Stop when your baby looks away, yawns or loses interest. Looking away is how a newborn says “enough for now” — and that is a complete class.

  5. 05

    Keep it short and calm

    Keep the experience short, calm and parent-led. Two to five minutes is plenty at this age, and you can always come back tomorrow.

Every baby develops differently. Ages on Kiddo School are guides, not tests or deadlines. If you ever have a question about your baby’s vision or development, your doctor or health visitor is the right person to ask.

THE LITTLE BIT OF LEARNING

Why black and white?

In the first weeks, most of what a newborn sees is soft and blurry, and strong black and white shapes are the easiest images for young eyes to notice. That is why high contrast cards and black and white baby flashcards have been a favourite newborn visual stimulation activity for generations. Following a slow-moving card gives your baby practice at focusing and tracking, and your voice turns the looking into language: circle, stripes, hello face. Nothing here is a lesson or a test — it is a calm minute of shared looking, at exactly your baby’s pace.
